# ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist

> For EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review. Answers reference specific paper sections.

---

## Section A: Did you describe the limitations of your work?

**A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work?**
Yes. See the dedicated Limitations section (§Limitations, after Conclusion). Key limitations discussed:
- Restricted to base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned models degrade substantially (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1=0.338 vs 0.763 base)
- Generators tested up to 8.2B parameters; frontier models (70B+) untested
- Prompt-type dependent: continuation chains strongest (0.781), paraphrastic weakest (0.671)
- Temperature sensitivity: method reliable at t≤0.7, degrades at t=0.9 (−9.3 to −26.0pp)
- English-only evaluation; non-English generalization untested
- 3-class granularity is the practical ceiling (5-class F1≈0.50)
- Reference model fixed to Pythia-410M (cross-reference spread 0.013 confirms not reference-specific)

**A2. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work?**
Yes. Ethics Statement discusses: (1) no personal/sensitive data involved, (2) method estimates depth not author identity, (3) potential misuse for suppressing legitimate AI-generated content, (4) recommended for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

**A3. Do your abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
Yes. Abstract states: DDR tri-partition finding, 7-feature ensemble binary F1=0.694 under LOGO, and instruction-tuning limitation. Introduction (§1) details the DDR tri-partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis.

---

## Section B: Did you use or create scientific artifacts?

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
Yes. All models cited: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software versions listed in Ethics Statement.

**B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Licenses: Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds).

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifacts is consistent with their intended use?**
Yes. All models used for text generation (intended use). Wikipedia used as seed text (public domain content).

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data/models contain information that names or uniquely identifies people or offensive content?**
Partially. Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated text is model output conditioned on these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?**
Yes. §3 (Method) fully documents: generation chain construction, feature extraction pipeline, evaluation protocol. Appendix provides dataset statistics (Appendix A), per-generator breakdowns, and ablation details. Code/data/models will be released upon publication.

---

## Section C: Did you run computational experiments?

**C1. Did you report the number of parameters in each model used?**
Yes. Table 1 lists parameter counts for all 8 generators (0.6B to 8.2B). Reference model: Pythia-410M (410M parameters). §3.2 specifies exact model identifiers.

**C2. Did you report the computing infrastructure used?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Compute budget: 4× NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total.

**C3. Did you report the average runtime for each approach?**
Partially. Table 2 reports inference time per text (ms/text): 7-feature ensemble 9.7ms, 4-detector ensemble 22.8ms. Training time not separately reported (XGBoost training is negligible, <1min per fold).

**C4. Did you report the evaluation metrics, along with the values and confidence intervals?**
Yes. All primary results include 95% bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Tables 1-2 report CIs. McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons (§4.2). Bonferroni correction applied within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes reported for DDR partition (§4.2).

**C5. Did you report the hyperparameter search strategy?**
Partially. XGBoost uses standard defaults (n_estimators=200, max_depth=6, lr=0.1) without hyperparameter search (§3.4). Appendix C shows alternative classifiers (CORAL, CORN, Frank-Hall) yield comparable performance, confirming discriminative power resides in features not classifier.

**C6. Did you report the number and range of values tried for each hyperparameter?**
N/A. No hyperparameter search conducted; default XGBoost parameters used throughout. Stability confirmed: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds (§3.4).

---

## Section D: Did you use or create data?

**D1. Did you discuss how the data was collected or created?**
Yes. §3.2 describes chain construction: ~1000 Wikipedia seed passages per generator, iterative continuation with fixed prompt template, temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max 256 tokens. 37,058 texts after removing 2,746 chain breaks and 11 short passages. Appendix A provides full dataset statistics.

**D2. Did you report the basic statistics of the data used?**
Yes. §3.2: total texts (37,058), chain breaks (2,746), depth distribution. Appendix A: per-generator breakdown, depth-class counts, token statistics.

**D3. Did you discuss if the data you are using/creating contains personally identifiable information or offensive content?**
Yes. Ethics Statement: "All texts analyzed are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no personal or sensitive data is involved."

**D4. Did you provide the data?**
Will release upon publication. Ethics Statement: "All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication."

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
5	Characterizing the structure of this evolution is fundamental to understanding how base language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with relevance to understanding model collapse dynamics \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}.
6	Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure this structure: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
7	
8	We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and term this \emph{depth profiling}.
9	No existing method provides a feature-level decomposition of depth signal in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
10	
11	The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a three-way partition: when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, three \emph{drifting} features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) shift monotonically (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), one \emph{intermediate} feature (entropy std) shows a non-monotonic level shift ($d{=}0.55$), and three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) exhibit negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$).
12	This is consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable under fixed sampling parameters.
13	While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured tri-partition and its exploitation for depth classification have not been previously reported.
14	We restrict to base (pretrained) models: by isolating the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, base models provide a controlled setting in which to study whether recursive distributional drift exhibits systematic structure (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
15	
16	A 7-feature ensemble combining all three groups achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M-parameter reference model (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
17	
18	Our contributions are empirical rather than methodological:
19	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
20	    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+, and construct an evaluation suite of 37{,}058 texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
Characterizing the structure of this evolution is fundamental to understanding how base language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with relevance to understanding model collapse dynamics \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}.
Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure this structure: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and term this \emph{depth profiling}.
No existing method provides a feature-level decomposition of depth signal in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a three-way partition: when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, three \emph{drifting} features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) shift monotonically (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), one \emph{intermediate} feature (entropy std) shows a non-monotonic level shift ($d{=}0.55$), and three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) exhibit negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$).
This is consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable under fixed sampling parameters.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured tri-partition and its exploitation for depth classification have not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models: by isolating the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, base models provide a controlled setting in which to study whether recursive distributional drift exhibits systematic structure (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

A 7-feature ensemble combining all three groups achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M-parameter reference model (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).

Our contributions are empirical rather than methodological:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+, and construct an evaluation suite of 37{,}058 texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) in base models: data-driven analysis reveals a primary drifting/non-drifting partition ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632); domain-informed criteria further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization (three drifting features, $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$; one intermediate, $d{=}0.55$; three near-stationary, $d < 0.10$) with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ effect-size gap confirmed under heteroscedasticity-robust metrics (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
    \item We map DDR's boundary conditions: the depth signal is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but attenuates at higher temperatures ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp at $t{=}0.9$). Instruction tuning compresses the DDR partition structure (silhouette: $0.632 \rightarrow 0.338$) rather than simply reversing feature directions; domain-specific retraining partially recovers within-model classification ($+$7--27\,pp) but cross-generator transfer remains weak (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Independent-Seed Control}
\label{app:seed-control}

To rule out topic-level leakage from shared seeds across generators, we construct an independent-seed evaluation where Pythia-2.8B and OLMo-2-1B use completely disjoint Wikipedia seed pools (500 seeds each, zero overlap).
Each generator produces depth-0 through depth-4 chains on its own seed pool; features are extracted with the same Pythia-410M reference model.
We then train a 7-feature XGBoost classifier on one generator's data and test on the other, in both directions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-2.8B $\rightarrow$ OLMo-2-1B & 0.695 & [0.673, 0.717] \\
OLMo-2-1B $\rightarrow$ Pythia-2.8B & 0.666 & [0.643, 0.689] \\
\midrule
Independent-seed average & 0.680 & --- \\
Shared-seed LOGO (reference) & 0.694 & [0.688, 0.700] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Independent-seed cross-generator evaluation (binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Disjoint seed pools eliminate any possibility of topic-based leakage. The average independent-seed F1 (0.680) is within 1.4\,pp of the shared-seed LOGO baseline (0.694). The classifier thus captures generative degradation patterns rather than seed-specific topic content.}
\label{tab:seed-control}
\end{table}

The small gap ($-$1.4\,pp) between independent-seed and shared-seed evaluation falls within bootstrap confidence intervals, and both directions individually exceed 0.66.
Combined with the seed-level demeaning control (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), these results provide converging evidence that depth classification is driven by distributional properties of recursive generation, not topic identity.

$H_{\max}$ & 0.01 & 0.16 & $-$0.04 & \textemdash & $-$0.08 & $-$0.13 & $-$0.15 \\

TTR & \textbf{0.86} & 0.43 & 0.20 & $-$0.13 & 0.13 & \textemdash & \textbf{0.97} \\
Hapax & \textbf{0.81} & 0.34 & 0.23 & $-$0.15 & 0.14 & \textbf{0.97} & \textemdash \\
\bottomrule

\end{table}

TTR and hapax ratio are near-perfectly correlated ($r=0.97$), and both correlate strongly with mean entropy ($r=0.86$ and $0.81$).
These three drifting features form a tightly coupled cluster: PCA on the standardized drifting-feature subset shows that a single principal component explains 92.3\% of their joint variance, with near-uniform loadings (0.56--0.59). These three features thus share a single latent dimension.
Full 7-feature PCA yields PC1 (44.4\% variance) loading on the drifting triplet (0.53--0.55) and PC2 (18.3\% variance) capturing entropy distributional shape (entropy std vs.\ entropy min contrast).
In contrast, $H_{\max}$, $\tau$ (tail decay), and $H_{\min}$ show weak pairwise correlations with all other features ($|r| < 0.27$); these features capture independent aspects of the token-probability distribution.

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.
We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Across eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$), intermediate, and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$) groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The DDR tri-partition is consistent with a location/shape decomposition: under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, the softmax output distribution's shape is constrained by decoding configuration, while iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location.
An informal conjecture is that temperature acts as a shape control parameter that bounds entropy spread, so recursive conditioning can shift the mean but not escape the shape constraint imposed by $\tau$; this would explain both high-temperature degradation and shape-feature stability.
This interpretation is post-hoc; formal analysis remains open.
DDR is a parameter-dependent empirical decomposition, not a universal property of recursive generation: ablations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) show degradation at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp) and variation across prompt types.

Instruction tuning fundamentally alters the depth signal across all three tested families (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}): entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign consistently ($-0.6$ base $\rightarrow$ $+0.23$ to $+0.48$ instruct), and retraining on instruction-tuned data partially recovers within-model binary F1 ($+$7--27\,pp) but remains below base-model levels (0.69--0.72).
The DDR partition structure itself degrades ($k{=}2$ silhouette: 0.632 $\rightarrow$ 0.338; cross-condition transfer near chance), restricting the structured partition to base models; within-model classification remains partially feasible with domain-specific retraining (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); a preliminary downstream pilot ($n{=}3$ seeds; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}) does not detect a depth-composition effect on training utility, though the sample size is insufficient for conclusions.

The QLoRA end-to-end classifier (3-class F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) confirms richer representations capture depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; the handcrafted ensemble trades classification ceiling for the interpretability that enables DDR decomposition.
Three classes represent the practical ceiling (5-class F1 ${\approx}$0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), with simulated editing suggesting graceful degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift is fully reversible and leaves distributional shape near-stationary ($d < 0.10$; variance ratios 0.98--1.12).
